details:
**Battle of the Zab and Marwan II**
The decisive 750 battle near the Great Zab River in Iraq where Abbasid forces defeated Marwan II, the last Umayyad caliph in Damascus. It brought the Abbasids to power, with Abu al-Abbas as-Saffah as their first caliph.

**Successor to the Umayyads**
The Abbasids replaced the Umayyad Caliphate in 750 as the third major Islamic caliphate. They were named after al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad. One surviving Umayyad, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Spain and founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

**Hulagu Khan and the 1258 Sack of Baghdad**
The Mongol commander Hulagu Khan destroyed Baghdad in 1258. According to legend, so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the river ran black with ink. The last Baghdad caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses, because the Mongols avoided spilling royal blood.

**House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma)**
The great library and translation center in Baghdad, associated with Harun al-Rashid and especially his son al-Ma'mun. It led the Graeco-Arabic translation movement, which put Greek, Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic, and it was destroyed in the 1258 Mongol sack.

**Harun al-Rashid**
The fifth Abbasid caliph (r. 786–809), whose reign is considered the dynasty's peak. He is a character in the One Thousand and One Nights, and according to Charlemagne's biographer Einhard he sent Charlemagne an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock.

**Battle of Talas River**
The 751 battle in Central Asia where Abbasid forces, helped by Karluk Turks who defected and by Tibetan allies, defeated a Tang Chinese army under Gao Xianzhi. It ended Tang expansion westward, and legend says that Chinese prisoners brought papermaking to Samarkand, from where it spread west.

**Abu Muslim and the Black Standard**
The Persian general who led the Abbasid Revolution from Khorasan, starting at Merv, under black banners. Despite his key role, he was murdered on the orders of the second caliph, al-Mansur, in 755.

**The Barmakids**
A Persian family from Balkh, originally administrators of a Buddhist monastery there, who served as powerful viziers to the early Abbasids. Yahya the Barmakid ran much of Harun al-Rashid's government before Harun abruptly purged the family in 803.

**Baghdad and al-Mansur**
The second caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad in 762 as the "City of Peace" (Madinat al-Salam), a round city on the Tigris, after facing revolts such as that of the Rawandiyya. It was the Abbasid capital and a center of world learning.

**Zanj Rebellion**
A huge revolt (869–883) of African slaves forced to labor in the salt marshes near Basra, led by Ali ibn Muhammad. It was eventually crushed by the caliph's brother and regent al-Muwaffaq.

**Anarchy at Samarra**
A chaotic period (861–870) that began with the murder of the caliph al-Mutawakkil by his Turkish guards. Four caliphs followed one another in about nine years while the Turkish military controlled the government from the new capital, Samarra.

**Mamluks and Turkish slave soldiers**
Al-Ma'mun and his brother al-Mu'tasim began using enslaved Turkish soldiers (mamluks or ghilman) as the core of the army. These soldiers later came to dominate the caliphs.

**Buyids and Seljuks**
The Shi'ite Persian Buyids took Baghdad in 945 and ruled the caliphs as figureheads for about a century. The Seljuk Turks replaced them in 1055. Other states broke away from Abbasid control, including the Tulunids, Saffarids, Samanids, Ghaznavids, Aghlabids and Idrisids.

**Fourth Fitna**
The civil war (811–813) between Harun al-Rashid's sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun. Al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated al-Amin's army at the Battle of Rayy, and al-Ma'mun took Baghdad.

**Islamic Golden Age scholars**
Scholars of the Abbasid era included al-Khwarizmi, whose treatise on al-jabr gave us the word "algebra" and who helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals; Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), whose Book of Optics rejected the emission theory of vision; and the Banu Musa brothers, authors of the Book of Ingenious Devices. After the Mongol sack, a line of Abbasid caliphs survived as figureheads in Mamluk Cairo until Ottoman Sultan Selim I removed al-Mutawakkil III in 1517.
